Jesus Freak
JEE-zus FREEK
noun (Boomer slang)
From Jesus + freak in its 1960s sense of a devotee or enthusiast ("a jazz freak"; the hippies called themselves "freaks"). Jesus freak appeared around 1969–71 for the converts of the Jesus Movement: long-haired former hippies and drug users who came to Christ through coffeehouses, beach baptisms, Calvary Chapel in Costa Mesa, and street evangelism. Time put "The Jesus Revolution" on its cover on June 21, 1971. The name began as mockery; many converts adopted it as a badge.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A Jesus freak was a convert of the early-1970s Jesus Movement: a hippie who had found Christ and could not stop talking about Him, with long hair, a big Bible, a "One Way" sign, and a zeal that embarrassed his parents’ church. Today the phrase means any intensely, openly devoted Christian. The Christian observation: the world has always thought such people were out of their minds. The Lord Jesus’ own family said, "He is beside himself" (Mar 3:21). Festus told Paul, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). The rulers of Thessalonica complained, "These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also" (Act 17:6). When the council saw Peter and John, "unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus" (Act 4:13). That is the honorable side of the name: Scripture commands a believer to be "fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11), and a cold, respectable Christianity is the stranger thing. But Paul also knew a zeal that goes wrong: "they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom 10:2). Some Jesus freaks burned bright and burned out; some drifted into cults that preyed on their enthusiasm. The lasting fruit came where the zeal was rooted in sound doctrine and a faithful church. Many pastors, missionaries, and Christian parents of today’s grandparent generation were Jesus freaks once. A family can honor that fire and pray that their children catch it — with knowledge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Early-1970s name, first mocking then embraced, for the zealous converts of the Jesus Movement — the kind of disciple the world has always called "beside himself" (Mar 3:21), whose zeal Scripture commands (Rom 12:11) but wants according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).

JESUS FREAK, n. (Boomer slang, c. 1969–71) A convert of the Jesus Movement, typically a former hippie, known for open, fervent devotion to Christ; hence any zealous, outspoken Christian. Often derisive at first; later adopted with pride.

Webster (1828) — ZEALOT, noun Zelot. One who engages warmly in any cause, and pursues his object with earnestness and ardor. It is generally used in dispraise, or applied to one whose ardor in intemperate and censurable. The fury of zealots was one cause of the destruction of Jerusalem.

Decode for families: if Grandpa was a Jesus freak in 1972, ask him to tell you how he came to faith. It will be worth hearing.

Key Scripture

Act 26:24 — "And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad."

Mar 3:21 — "And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself."

Act 17:6 — "And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;"

Act 4:13 — "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus."

Rom 12:11 — "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;"

Rom 10:2 — "For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge."

Modern Corruption

The world mocks zeal for Christ as madness, as it always has; Scripture commands fervent spirit but warns that zeal without knowledge can go astray.

expand to see more

The mockery in the name is the mockery of Festus. The world does not mind religion that stays polite; it minds a young man who has met Jesus and talks about Him at the gas station. The Jesus Movement embarrassed many established churches, which could not decide whether to welcome long-haired converts or require them to cut their hair first. Some churches welcomed them, and grew; others did not, and the converts went elsewhere. The lesson for congregations is permanent: do not quench real zeal because it arrives looking strange.

The other lesson is Paul’s in Rom 10:2. Zeal is a fire; it needs a hearth. Without teaching, accountability, and the ordinary means of grace, the hottest convert can burn out or be captured by a cult — and some in the early 1970s were. The best fruit of the Jesus Movement came where enthusiasm met doctrine: men and women who are still in the pew fifty years later, still fervent, now also wise.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Jesus (Greek Iēsous, Hebrew Yeshua, "the LORD saves") + 1960s freak (devotee) → Jesus freak, c. 1969–71; Time, "The Jesus Revolution," June 21, 1971.
